Most Artificial Intelligence Glaucoma Studies Lack Clear Diagnostic Criteria Review Finds

A systematic review of contemporary artificial intelligence research in glaucoma has revealed that fewer than thirty percent of published studies explicitly define the diagnostic criteria used to identify the disease, exposing critical inconsistencies in ground truth labeling across medical machine learning datasets. In an analysis examining one hundred and sixty peer-reviewed investigations published in 2025 and 2026, researchers found that one hundred and fourteen articles, representing 71.2 percent of the evaluated literature, failed to provide any explicit clinical definition or standardized diagnostic threshold for confirming glaucoma cases within their experimental cohorts. Only forty-six studies, or 28.8 percent, clearly articulated the diagnostic parameters applied during model development or validation. Among this minority that reported diagnostic baselines, the investigators identified thirty-eight distinct definitions, demonstrating an absence of consensus that threatens the reproducibility, clinical validity, and generalizability of diagnostic algorithms designed to detect visual impairment.

The findings arrive amid an exponential surge in algorithmic healthcare applications, with ophthalmic diagnostics representing one of the most rapidly expanding commercial and scientific sectors. Artificial intelligence technologies are increasingly being explored to augment clinical practice and relieve intensifying workloads driven by worldwide physician shortages. Bibliometric data indicate that between 2020 and 2024, researchers published 21,725 scientific articles dedicated to artificial intelligence applications in ophthalmology, with glaucoma emerging as the second most studied ophthalmic pathology in algorithmic research. Financially, the global market for ophthalmic artificial intelligence applications was valued at approximately 283 million United States dollars in 2025 and is projected to climb to 4.4 billion dollars by 2034. As software developers and clinical researchers direct computational resources toward automated disease detection, risk stratification, progression monitoring, surgical outcome prediction, and complication forecasting, the rigor of underlying reference standards becomes decisive for patient safety.

Defining glaucoma has historically presented substantial clinical difficulties even among experienced ophthalmic subspecialists, creating deep-seated methodological challenges that current algorithmic research now inherits. Classical clinical frameworks initially characterized glaucoma as optic nerve damage arising primarily in the setting of pathologically elevated intraocular pressure. However, the subsequent recognition of normal-tension glaucoma disrupted this singular paradigm, compelling international professional bodies, including the American Academy of Ophthalmology and the European Glaucoma Society, to formulate comprehensive diagnostic guidelines centered on concurrent structural optic nerve alterations and corresponding visual field deficits. Despite these authoritative guidelines, diagnostic variability remains entrenched across traditional clinical research as well as algorithmic literature. A separate 2026 systematic review evaluating eighty-three randomized controlled trials identified more than fifty-seven distinct diagnostic definitions of glaucoma across the medical literature, indicating that the diagnostic ambiguity observed in computational modeling reflects an enduring, unresolved controversy across ophthalmic science.

To evaluate how contemporary machine learning investigations navigate this diagnostic complexity, investigators from the Department of Ophthalmology at the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill conducted a systematic literature review following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis 2020 guidelines. Using medical subject headings terms for glaucoma and artificial intelligence, the authors queried PubMed on June 14, 2026, capturing machine learning, deep learning, and neural network applications. The authors excluded reviews, editorial letters, conference proceedings, non-human investigations, and studies examining pediatric, angle-closure, or secondary glaucoma due to their disparate pathophysiological mechanisms. The initial search yielded 300 publications, from which the reviewers excluded 140 articles: twenty due to publication type, ninety-one for lacking relevant subject matter, fifteen for focusing on angle-closure or secondary glaucoma, three for examining pediatric populations, and eleven for using non-human data. Ultimately, 160 studies involving human subjects aged 18 and older met inclusion criteria.

Across the 160 included investigations, the research team analyzed the primary clinical and technical domains targeted by the underlying machine learning models. Fundus photograph interpretation constituted the most frequent focus, accounting for seventy articles or 43.8 percent of the analyzed cohort. Multi-modal diagnostic applications, which integrate multiple imaging or clinical data streams, represented thirty-two studies, or 20.0 percent, while optical coherence tomography diagnostics formed the primary subject of twenty-five studies, or 15.6 percent. Beyond structural imaging, ten studies, representing 6.3 percent, focused on genetics and genomics, eight studies, or 5.0 percent, applied text-based analyses to electronic medical records or clinical case descriptions, and seven studies, or 4.4 percent, concentrated exclusively on visual field evaluations. Less frequent focal areas included risk factor and complication prediction across four studies, anterior segment slit-lamp photography across two studies, and corneal biomechanics in a single investigation.

Among the forty-six studies that documented explicit diagnostic criteria, the authors categorized the thirty-eight unique definitions into five mutually exclusive classifications based on their incorporated diagnostic domains. The vast majority of these studies, totaling twenty-nine publications or 63.0 percent, utilized mixed criteria that combined two diagnostic domains, such as pairing visual field testing with optic disc evaluation, without encompassing all three fundamental domains of pressure, structure, and functional testing. Visual field-related criteria formed the second largest group, encompassing nine studies, or 19.6 percent, which prioritized functional testing deficits. Imaging-focused definitions, which prioritized structural parameters derived from fundus photography or optical coherence tomography, accounted for four studies, or 8.7 percent. In contrast, combined comprehensive criteria requiring all three elements—intraocular pressure, structural optic nerve head or retinal nerve fiber layer assessments, and functional visual fields—were utilized by only three studies, or 6.5 percent. A single study, representing 2.2 percent, relied primarily on intraocular pressure-emphasized criteria.

An granular examination of the specific diagnostic parameters incorporated within those forty-six defined protocols highlighted stark disparities in how researchers verify disease presence. Humphrey visual field mean deviation appeared most frequently, incorporated in thirty-six studies, or 78.3 percent of defined definitions. Retinal nerve fiber layer assessment was documented in twenty-seven studies, representing 58.7 percent, while hemifield testing or pattern standard deviation and cup-to-disc ratio criteria were each employed by twenty studies, or 43.5 percent. Conversely, elevated intraocular pressure appeared in only ten studies, representing 21.7 percent, and gonioscopic assessment of the anterior chamber angle was required in just six studies, or 13.0 percent.
